subject: Biotechnology
title: Plastic-Eating Microbes
description: A short lesson to help you apply Plastic-Eating Microbes.

hook.text: 350 million tons of plastic produced annually — in 2016 scientists found bacteria that evolved to eat PET plastic bottles.

buildup.text: Ideonella sakaiensis produces PETase — an enzyme that breaks PET into terephthalic acid and ethylene glycol, its building blocks.

discovery.text: Engineered super-PETase degrades PET six times faster than the wild enzyme — protein engineering accelerates nature's solution.

twist.text: PET is only one of seven common plastics — polyethylene and polypropylene remain largely resistant to biological degradation.

climax.text: Carbios uses engineered enzymes to recycle PET bottles into new bottles — enzymatic recycling achieves true circular plastics.

punchline.text: Bacteria evolved to eat our trash — enzymatic recycling may close the plastic loop.

quiz.question: What limitation exists for enzyme-based plastic degradation?
options: Enzymes can only degrade plastics at extremely high temperatures
Current enzymes primarily work on PET, while polyethylene and polypropylene remain largely resistant to biological breakdown
Enzyme-based degradation produces toxic byproducts that are worse than the original plastic

details.summary: Certain bacteria and fungi produce enzymes that break down plastic polymers, including PET, polyethylene, and polystyrene. Ideonella sakaiensis was discovered in 2016 digesting PET bottles, and engineered variants now degrade plastics significantly faster than the wild-type organism.

faq.question: Can bacteria actually eat and fully digest plastic?
faq.answer: Ideonella sakaiensis breaks PET into terephthalic acid and ethylene glycol monomers using PETase and MHETase enzymes, then metabolizes these products for energy. The process fully mineralizes PET to CO2 and water, though at rates still too slow for industrial waste processing.

faq.question: How far is enzyme-based plastic recycling from commercial reality?
faq.answer: Carbios launched a demonstration plant in 2023 that enzymatically recycles PET bottles into virgin-quality monomers. The process handles colored, contaminated, and mixed PET waste that mechanical recycling cannot. Full commercial plants are planned for 2025 with major brand partnerships.
